summary: A 1975 survey of the state of New-Protocol Telnet servers, listing which sites had which features working. It is a status snapshot. It updates RFC 701, RFC 702 and RFC 669; see also RFC 703.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the February 1975 headcount of which ARPANET computers had switched to the new Telnet and which had not. Half had made the change, and the author sounds disappointed at how slow it is going.

questions: new protocol telnet servers on socket 27
how many arpanet hosts had new telnet in 1975
subtitle: The February 1975 progress check on new-protocol Telnet servers, with progress even slower than before.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET community was still waiting for server hosts to move from the old Telnet protocol to the new one.
tldr.mechanism: D. W. Dodds re-ran the survey from the new-protocol user Telnet at BBNA as of 20 February 1975, listed what had changed, and updated the summary and the host table.
tldr.outcome: 18 of 36 server hosts, half of them, had a new-protocol implementation, yet the author calls the progress even slower than before. The unit metadata lists RFC 669 as updated by it and RFC 703 as updating it.

today: RFC 679 is a snapshot from early 1975. The unit metadata gives its status as unknown, lists RFC 669 among the RFCs it updates and RFC 703 as an update to it.

sections.title: What Changed Since the Last Survey
sections.content:
The report comes two and a half months after the previous one, and the author finds it depressing that progress toward an all-new-protocol network has been even slower than before. Host numbers are given in octal.

SRI-ARC (2) and OFFICE-1 (53) added a logger socket 27, but still with old-protocol servers. LL-67 (12) now has a new-protocol server on socket 1. SDC-CC (110) was removed from the list until it starts operating on the network, and CASE-10 (15) left the network. BBN-TENEX is now host 361, formerly 105. ANL (Argonne, 67) joined with old-protocol and new-protocol servers on sockets 1 and 27.
sections.plainLanguage: First the note lists which computers joined, left or changed since the last check. The author is not pleased with the pace.

sections.title: The Summary Counts
sections.content:
There were 36 total server hosts. Of them, 17, or 47 percent, had no new-protocol server; 1, or 3 percent, was of unknown status because it was a new host; and 18, or 50 percent, had a new-protocol implementation.

Within those 18, 10 (28 percent) ran the new protocol on socket 27 with the old one on socket 1, 6 (16 percent) ran it on both socket 1 and socket 27, and 2 (6 percent) ran it on socket 1 only. All of the data were gathered by a surveying program plus a few manual checks, as seen by the new-protocol user Telnet at BBNA on 20 February 1975.
sections.plainLanguage: Of 36 computers, 18 had the new version working and 17 did not. The numbers are arranged so you can see which socket each one used.

sections.title: The Table and Its Options
sections.content:
The tabulation lists each server site by host number and name, with an entry for socket 1 and socket 27 and the new-protocol options implemented. X means no server at that socket and ? means the status could not be found, usually because the host could not be reached.

An I# entry means option number # is implemented incoming to the user, so the server says Will #, and an O# entry means it is implemented outgoing from the user, so the server says Do #. The options implemented by anyone are 0 Transmit-Binary, 1 Echo, 3 Suppress-Go-Ahead and 6 Timing-Mark. The RFC adds a note that one server, SU-AI, returns improper responses to some option requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is a report card with a row for each computer and columns for which extra features it can handle. A short key explains the letters and numbers.

references.text: Dodds, D. W., "November, 1974, Survey of New-Protocol TELNET Servers", RFC 669, December 1974.
